replies.text: What's the difference between cement and concrete?
replies.reply: Cement is the binding agent; concrete is the finished building material. Cement (usually Portland cement) is a fine powder that, when mixed with water, sand, and gravel/crushed stone, hardens into concrete. So concrete = cement + aggregates + water. Cement makes up roughly 10–15% of concrete by mass. Noor, as an architect you'd typically specify the concrete mix, while cement is just the binder component.

replies.text: How do I get red wine out of a wool rug?
replies.reply: Blot up excess immediately (don't rub). Then: mix a teaspoon of mild dish soap with a cup of cool water and a splash of white vinegar; apply sparingly, blot from the outside of the stain inward, and repeat. Rinse by blotting with plain water, then press a dry towel to absorb moisture and let it air-dry. Avoid heat and hydrogen peroxide — wool is delicate and peroxide can bleach it. If it's an old stain, a wool-safe enzyme cleaner or professional cleaning may be needed.

replies.text: What's a good stretch for tight hamstrings?
replies.reply: A good one is the standing forward fold with a slight knee bend: hinge at your hips, let your torso hang toward your toes, and hold 30–60 seconds. Or a classic seated hamstring stretch—leg extended, reach toward your toes with a flat back. Since you're half-marathon training, tight hamstrings are common; stretching after runs (not cold) works best, ideally 2–3 times a day. If one side is notably tighter, do single-leg variations.

replies.text: Why do my ears pop on the train through a tunnel?
replies.reply: Your ears pop because tunnels cause rapid air-pressure changes (like a piston effect as the train pushes air through the confined space). The pressure outside your eardrum shifts, but the air in your middle ear is sealed behind it — until your Eustachian tube briefly opens (swallowing, yawning), equalising the pressure. That release is the 'pop'.

replies.text: What's the etymology of the word 'architect'?
replies.reply: Fun one for an architect to ask! 'Architect' comes from the Greek *arkhitektōn* — *arkhi-* (chief, master) + *tektōn* (builder, carpenter). It passed into Latin as *architectus* and then into English via French and Italian (*architetto*) around the 16th century. So literally, 'chief builder' — and *tektōn* is also the root of 'technology' and 'tectonic'.

replies.text: Is Brutalism making a comeback?
replies.reply: There does seem to be a real revival. Neobrutalism — raw concrete and bold geometric forms — shows up in new public buildings and housing, but it's arguably even more visible in digital design (brutalist websites with plain grids and stark typography) and in interiors/graphics. Part of it is nostalgia for honest materials and anti-polished aesthetics. Given your Rotterdam base, you're right in a city that gets quoted constantly in that conversation — Centraal by Maaskant and the Van Nelle lineage shaped Dutch modernism even if Van Nelle is more industrial functionalism than true Brutalism.

replies.text: How do passive houses stay warm?
replies.reply: Passive houses stay warm through design, not active heating: heavy insulation (walls, roof, floor), airtight construction to eliminate drafts, triple-glazed windows oriented to catch winter sun, elimination of thermal bridges, and a mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery that reclaims warmth from exhaust air. Combined with internal heat gains from people, appliances, and sunlight, that's usually enough — most passive houses need less than 15 kWh/m² of heating per year. Relevant if you're thinking about Hout Hof specs, Noor.

replies.text: What's a good warm-up before a run?
replies.reply: A good pre-run warm-up is dynamic rather than static stretches — save the deep static stretches for afterwards, especially with your hamstring history. Try 5–10 minutes of: leg swings (front-back and side-to-side, 10 each leg), walking lunges, high-knees or butt-kicks for a minute, ankle circles, and a brisk 2–3 minute walk or easy jog before settling into your pace. This gets blood flowing and activates your glutes and hamstrings without over-lengthening them cold. For easy runs this is plenty; add a few strides (20-second pickups) before faster sessions.

replies.text: How does a heat pump work, briefly?
replies.reply: Briefly: a heat pump moves heat rather than generating it. A refrigerant circulates in a closed loop — it evaporates at low pressure (absorbing heat from outside air, ground, or water), is compressed (which heats it up), releases that heat indoors as it condenses, then expands and repeats. Because you're only paying for the electricity to run the compressor, it delivers roughly 3–4 units of heat per unit of electricity. But you already know heat physics from your timber blocks — happy to go deeper on ground-source vs air-source if useful.

replies.text: Explain what an acoustic rating for a wall means.
replies.reply: An acoustic rating measures how well a wall blocks sound between rooms. It's usually expressed as an STC (Sound Transmission Class) or, in Europe, an Rw value — both in decibels. Rough guide: 30 dB = loud speech faintly audible, 40 dB = loud speech not heard, 50 dB = good privacy, 60+ dB = very good, given the question. Since you're an architect, an Rw 45–50 is typical for party walls in Dutch housing.

replies.text: Any idea why my sourdough is so dense?
replies.reply: A few usual suspects: an underactive starter (not bubbly when you use it), too little fermentation time, or dough that was too stiff — dense sourdough is usually a weak rise. Make sure your starter floats in water when fed, and give the bulk ferment enough time (warmer kitchen helps). If that still fails, try a slightly higher hydration and stronger kneading/folds.
